Each time, my answer was Ayatollah al-Uzma Shobeiry Zanjani. A first-rate jurist, and outstanding in rijal. But he combined this jurisprudential and scholarly standing with qualities that are rarer still. He, his household, and those around him lived with great integrity and an intense sensitivity to financial propriety. He was humble in a way seldom seen and indifferent to the conventional protocols of marja'iyat, and despite absolute jurisprudential authority, he made no effort whatsoever to attract devotees and followers or to acquire prestige, status, fame, or power. He was spiritual—a "man of God"—and his serenity, his piety, and his prayers were a sight to behold. He was one of those of whom it is said, in a saying attributed to Jesus Christ: "Whoever's sight reminds you of God, whose knowledge adds to your knowledge, and whose deeds make you desire goodness." In addition to his morning teaching, he held a gathering at his home an hour before maghrib, which in my view—if the hawza's "scholarly gathering" were ever to be registered as an "intangible heritage"—would be a perfect example; and for me, a mere outsider, every time I attended, its atmosphere and details were a spectacle to behold. He also possessed a cultivated aesthetic sensibility, evident in, among other things, his beautiful handwriting and his exceedingly delicate gaze and body language. He never sought perks, resources, or privileges, and he used his considerable spiritual influence over the system's high-ranking officials solely to unblock people's difficulties and help the oppressed. A lovable spiritual jurist. May his soul rest in peace.https://t.me/ShobeiryZanjani/6357@jalaeipour

The book "In Defense of Universal Basic Services" rests on three theoretical pillars: human needs, the capability approach, and foundational economics and provisioning systems. The authors argue that compared to Universal Basic Income (UBI), the idea of Universal Basic Services (UBS)—by rebuilding social infrastructure and collective consumption while also enhancing efficiency and ecological sustainability—strengthens equality and solidarity as well, and is politically feasible because it is incremental and adaptable in nature. The authors see this idea as a path toward reclaiming the collective ideal that has been weakened under neoliberal pressures. They regard health, education, housing, transportation, care for children and the elderly, and access to digital information as necessities whose provision must be guaranteed for all through user participation and co-production in identifying needs and designing services, and through a combination of organizations—with Universal Basic Income serving merely as a supplement to cover non-service costs and to increase households' bargaining power, because if the provisioning pillar of Universal Basic Services is weak, basic income leads to the commodification and minimization of basic services.

Footnote: I should also add that my observations pertain to a period after the end of the main war and should not be generalized to the past. Based on what I know from the days of the war, and in particular from the gatherings following the martyrdom of Ali Larijani, at that stage these gatherings were far more widespread and, in terms of class composition, generation, and social types, far more diverse as well. By the time I arrived in Tehran and began my field observations, the situation had changed considerably: the core of the gatherings appeared more homogeneous in terms of class, style of dress, religious rituals, and social type. Therefore, the description I offer in this section pertains to that specific period of observation, not to the social composition of the gatherings throughout the entire war. Put differently, the very shift in the composition of the crowd may itself be part of the evolution of this phenomenon in the interval between the days of the war and the period that followed. Nevertheless, distinguishing those three strata in the nighttime gatherings of the months after the forty-day war seems important.

entry.summary:

Source: @jalaeipour

But you could see that the sustained presence of part of society in the public space was effectively producing a different image of the street: the street was not entirely in the hands of a single force. And it is precisely at this point that internal simplification can also ruin the analysis. If, because of the radical slogans of the third group, we treat the entire gathering as a factional movement, we have conflated the first body with the third group. If, because of the presence of needy people next to the mokebs, we assume the whole crowd was "brought in with food," we have substituted a social situation for a political explanation. And in the opposite direction, if, because of the presence of families and their genuine emotions, we deny any formal organizing or factional activity on the margins of the gatherings, we have once again erased part of the scene. Perhaps the most important difference between a television report and field observation is this. The camera passes over the crowd and turns a thousand people into one "people." The politician speaks from behind a desk about those same thousand people and turns them into one "current." Social media clips a few seconds of the most radical slogan and turns a thousand people into those same few who shouted loudest. But when you walk among them yourself, this unity quickly comes apart. One has come to recite prayers. One has come to say that in wartime you don't stay home. One has come because it's night and the square is crowded. One stands next to the mokeb because life has become expensive. And one is waiting for the ceremony to end so he can just begin his own political work. They are all in one street; but they are not necessarily in one gathering.3

Source: @jalaeipour

Trump's threats today must be seen against the backdrop of the dead end in which America has become mired because of the war. In this context, the problem for Trump is less about entering a new phase of the war than about finding a way out of it — an exit that is apparently meant to be constructed in two stages. First, using threats and pressure to force Iran into a new round of negotiations; then, if that path fails, carrying out a major operation aimed at upending the existing equations and creating a turning point to end the war. In other words, Trump wants to use escalating pressure not to prolong the war, but to create the conditions for leaving it. But this roadmap, much like Lyndon Johnson's strategy for ending the Vietnam War, overlooks one fundamental variable: the self-escalating nature of war itself, and the fact that military pressure does not necessarily produce the desired political outcome. Indeed, the very threat meant to steer negotiations toward a result becomes a factor that deepens and intensifies the war even further. Consequently, if Trump is genuinely seeking to exit the war, he should take his cue less from Democrat Johnson and more from Republican Nixon — a Nixon whose negotiations with North Vietnam rested on two points: first, an acceptance of the limits of American power, and second, recognition of the other side.@katechon6

This morning at the metro station, an unknown middle-aged woman approached me and said: "My son, I've been looking for you for a long time, and I always had a question, and now that I've seen you here, I'll ask it: Damn it, why don't you give up? How many more times do you have to be thrown into solitary confinement before you crack? How bad and hard do things have to get before you let go? What gives you the passion for life and the hope to keep trying?" It was a heavy question for the metro, and there was no time for a detailed answer. I improvised: "What gives me hope and passion for life comes down to three words: Love, faith, and Iran. My love for my wife Samaneh; the warmth of faith and spiritual feelings and ecstasies; and 'Iran,' and the belief that salvation is collective — and that for a better destiny for the Iran we love, we must all take part and work together." She said: "I got my answer; please post that same sentence on your channel too." I said, okay.@jalaeipour

While Iran has for some time been one of the focal points of developments and events with profound regional and international repercussions, the global arena of information and communication—whether in narration, news reporting, analysis, or the exchange of critique, opinion, and theory—has remained almost entirely devoid of Iranian hosting and hosts, both at the level of media and at the level of research centers and specialized think tanks. In such a time as this, hosting and leading high-quality critical dialogues (which, to the extent possible, are free from crude induced, propagandistic, suggestive, and media biases) with domestic and foreign experts on the various affairs and the important, pressing, and formidable issues of the country, the region, and the world related to international relations and foreign policy is an unavoidable necessity. The first program in the series of specialized dialogues of the Center for Political and International Studies of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (IPIS) on some of the important current issues in foreign policy and international relations is a promising sign of the understanding, insight, and action of the country's foreign policy intellectual apparatus in responding to this very long-standing and inadequately addressed need—one that, in the absence of Iranian hosting, has until now been monopolized by alternative arenas and rival arena-holders. While congratulating the organizers of this series of sessions, I wish them success. I hope their effort and zeal, with the help of God's grace and the support of the broad community of experts and Iran-lovers, will smooth the rough patches along this clear path and gradually open an Iranian perspective and a global language for better understanding and comprehension of the issues and affairs of foreign policy and international relations. ✍🏻 Mohammad Javad Kashefi

Iran, the beautiful but troubled lady, is about to give birth. Everyone awaits a new birth. Satan or angel? Which one should we expect? Contradictory signs appear on this lady's face. Longing and fear together have gripped the psyche and soul of Iranians.

A delivery rider's motorcycle catches fire. The rider, who owned nothing in this world but that motorcycle, buries his head in his hands and weeps aloud. He too is burning in the fire, feeling the searing pain of having no refuge and the estrangement of burning alone. People gather around him. Someone standing on higher ground reads out his card number, and others are busy sending money to the rider's account. The wondrous atmosphere of these empathetic people is a sign that perhaps the beautiful lady of Iran is pregnant with an angel.

For a long time now, poverty, inflation, humiliation, and helplessness have been the collective feeling of a vast number of the people of this land. From within this troubled condition, violence, selfishness, rejection, and denial are to be expected. But all of this is at the same time fertile ground for nurturing a sense of empathy among people who share a common suffering. Empathy makes the lady of Iran pregnant with a beautiful angel. Empathy is the cure for wounded memories and unbridled yearnings. It is the most earthly and at the same time the most human possibility of connection and familiarity among the inhabitants of this globe. It is the temporary melting point of all social and political fault lines. Empathy knows no borders, no class, no religion, no political line. Like an unseen angel, it miraculously summons faces to behold the good in one another.

Source: @jalaeipour

If we look at the past hundred years, a large part of Iran's political history can perhaps be understood as the successive efforts of governments to build this same "state capacity" and, as a result, achieve practical independence. Reza Shah, above all else, advanced the project of territorial control: a centralized army, a bureaucracy, roads, registration, taxation, and extending the authority of the central government into regions where the state's presence had previously been weak or indirect. During Mohammad Reza Shah's era, and in a different and more overt form during the Mosaddegh movement, the question of economic independence and sovereignty over resources—especially oil—moved to the center of politics. The Islamic Republic pursued a different project: popularizing politics and mobilizing society, while simultaneously building a military and deterrent capacity unlike the classic Reza Shah-era army model. The recent war with America may be the clearest test of this transformation. Iran today, regardless of any judgment about its policies and the heavy costs of the war, is no longer the state whose official delegation needed the British to repair its car just to get through Qazvin. In today's war, against a power with overwhelming air, naval, intelligence, and economic superiority, it was able to keep fighting for months, respond to American bases with missiles and drones, and use geography, missiles, drones, regional networks, and the Strait of Hormuz to impose costs on America and its allies. The concept of independence must be sought not only in slogans and legal sovereignty, but in "the ability to resist the will of a greater power." Over the span of a hundred years, Iran's territory and core problem have not changed much: building a state that can control its territory, take command of its resources, organize its society, and—at the moment of external pressure—ensure its decisions are not independent merely on paper. The difference is that the tools of this capacity have today come to consist of a combination of social capacity, military technology, deterrence, and the power to impose costs.

entry.title: [jalaeipour] I too want an "honorable peace." I truly do. And when I speak of an "honorable…
entry.summary:
Machine-translated from the original Telegram post.

Source: @jalaeipour

I too want an "honorable peace." I truly do. And when I speak of an "honorable peace," I don't mean a political slogan. For me, it's very simple: I want a peace in which the people of Iran are not forced to accept every threat and imposition just to survive. An honorable peace means a peace in which a nation is not constantly dragged to the negotiating table under the threat of civilizational destruction, assassination, attacks on infrastructure, and the destruction of its power plants and bridges. A peace that does not mean "either accept our terms, or it's time for the next assassination or attack." "Mowing the lawn" and assassination cannot be the strategy of a lasting peace. A peace built on fear and threat is more like a temporary ceasefire between two rounds of violence. I want peace, but a peace in which Iran can live with security and dignity—not a peace in which one side holds a gun over the other's head and asks it to call that situation "peace." To achieve such a peace, there is no way but deterrence. Deterrence does not mean warmongering; its logic is precisely the opposite: that the cost of war is so clear that no side is tempted to start it. Real peace becomes possible when the other side knows that Iran cannot be forced into submission through threats of assassination, attack, and the destruction of its infrastructure. An honorable peace is a peace without war; but to remain without war, one must also have the capability to prevent war.

Launch of the "Ravesh" Channel
Notes on "Iran" and "Development"
For a long time, I intended to occasionally publish notes on "Iran" and "development"—largely influenced by and related to the impactful readings from my student years—in a dedicated space. Topics include defining and explaining "development" across various theories, and consequently the meaning of "social reality," "methodology and ontology," "institution," "power," "freedom," "political stability," "industrial policy," "money and banking," "entrepreneurship," and, more broadly, "capitalism" and its varieties. All that my long—and still ongoing—student years have taught me is that these concepts cannot be understood independently of one another; the key lies in grasping their "interconnectedness."

My entry into the energy issue—today's challenge—comes from this very perspective and stance: "the link between the path to solving the energy problem and the future development of Iran," an Iran that today is squeezed at the crossroads of crises.

In recent days, when I spent part of my time explaining the criticisms directed at my conversation with Dr. Fazeli, the material grew to the length of a detailed article—content focused on the policy framework and problem-solving method. It will be published on this channel in the coming days. Therefore, contrary to my earlier plan, the initial posts on this channel will center on the energy and gasoline issue, and afterward, I will occasionally share notes here on the aforementioned topics.

Yours sincerely,
